whyThisMatters: IT Support is not just the team people call when something looks wrong — you are also a target. Your accounts open more doors than most, so attackers spend extra effort making tickets, vendor calls, and system alerts look like the ones you handle every day. Today you will build the habit of checking the channel and the domain before you act, even when a request already looks like routine IT work.
rememberThis: A ticket number, a familiar tool's look, or a caller who knows the right jargon is not proof. STOP and check the actual sending domain and channel before you install anything, grant access, or re-enter a password — VERIFY through a number or console you already trust, then REPORT anything that pushed you to skip that step.

discussionPrompts: Ask how many people on the team check the sending domain on a ticket-notification email versus just trusting the ticket number and subject line.
For the system alert card, ask what a genuine urgent alert from your own monitoring tools actually looks like — does it ever ask you to re-enter your password through a link?
Ask what your team's real process is for a request to bypass change-approval 'just this once' — who is actually allowed to authorise that, and how would you check?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often miss the escalation-ticket card because the ticket number and internal jargon look right, and the request to help fast feels like the job. The habit to build is the same one used everywhere else: check the exact sending domain, and treat any request to skip verification or install an unapproved tool as the actual red flag, not the urgency itself.

items.title: Real vs Fake Escalation Ticket Notification
items.whatIsWrong: The fake ticket comes from helpdesk@synergymarine-support.com — a different domain from the real helpdesk@synergymarinegroup.com. Its ticket number format is also broken (#48213-A instead of IT-48213), and it asks you to install an unapproved remote-access tool, grant admin access, and skip the normal change-approval step because a director supposedly escalated it directly.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Genuine escalations keep the same ticket-ID format you already use and never ask you to bypass change-approval or install a tool you were not already trained on, no matter who is named as asking. A named senior title attached to urgency is exactly the pressure this trick relies on — verify by calling the requester back on a known internal extension, or checking the ticket in the console directly, before installing anything or granting access.

items.title: Real vs Fake Admin Console Alert
items.whatIsWrong: The fake alert comes from alerts@synergymarine-monitor.net, not your real monitoring tool's synergymarinegroup.com address. It invents a 5-minute countdown (the real one gives you 24 hours) and puts a "Re-authenticate now" button that sends your admin username and password to a lookalike domain, instead of pointing you to the console you already have bookmarked.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Your own monitoring tool never asks for your password through a link in an alert email — it gives you time and directs you to the URL you already use. Admin credentials are a high-value target precisely because they open more than a normal account, so attackers copy the exact look of your own tools and add panic to make you skip that check. Always re-authenticate by opening the console yourself, never by clicking the link in the alert.

items.title: Real vs Fake Vendor Patch Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (sailorlink-support.net vs sailorlink-comms.com). It asks you to download and run a patch directly, and explicitly tells you to skip your own IT verification steps because it "comes directly from" the vendor.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real vendor patches always go through your own vetted deployment process, never a direct download link in an unsolicited email — and no genuine vendor ever tells you to skip your own team's verification steps. An outage threat is the pressure lever designed to make you act before checking.

items.title: Real vs Fake Employee Reset Request
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from a different domain (synergymarine-mail.com vs synergymarinegroup.com — not the employee's real company address). It explicitly asks to skip standard identity verification, and asks for the new password to be emailed directly instead of through the secure reset channel.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A genuine employee's request always comes from their real company address and goes through the ticket or self-service process. An explicit request to skip verification is the same social-engineering pattern whether it arrives by phone or by email — the channel changes, the red flag doesn't.

items.title: Real vs Fake Credential Vault Alert
items.whatIsWrong: The fake alert comes from a different domain (synergy-vaultaccess.net vs synergymarinegroup.com). It invents a 5-minute deadline and a device-flag story, then asks you to re-enter your master vault password through a link instead of the vault console you already use.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A credential vault holding privileged access is one of the highest-value targets in the whole environment — a genuine vault alert gives you time and points you back to its own console, never a link asking for your master password. The device-flag story is designed to make the urgency feel technical and credible.
